text: Chapter 5 covered Extract and Load in isolation, against a real database. This chapter builds all three ETL stages into one real, running pipeline — and this lesson is about how to structure it before writing a line of cleaning logic.

Every ETL pipeline does the same three things, in order. Extract pulls raw data from a source. Transform cleans it, validates it, and reshapes it into the form the target expects. Load writes the result somewhere it can be used. The order matters — you can't clean data you haven't pulled yet.

This chapter's running example is orders.csv — twenty real rows for an outdoor-gear retailer. It's not artificially clean. Row 1005 is missing a customer name, and row 1014 has a quantity of negative one. Real source data looks like this far more often than it looks tidy, which is exactly why Transform needs to be its own deliberate stage.

Structure the pipeline as one function per stage. extract reads the CSV. transform drops rows missing a customer name and drops non-positive quantities. load writes the cleaned result out. Each function does exactly one job and only knows about its own input and output — that's what makes each stage independently testable later, in Chapter 7.

The orchestrator ties it together: call extract, hand its output to transform, hand that output to load, then report how many rows made it through. It doesn't contain any cleaning logic itself — it just describes the pipeline, stage by stage.

Why bother separating things at all? A single giant function that reads, cleans, and writes all in one block works right up until something breaks — then you can't tell if the bug is in reading, cleaning, or writing. Next lesson, we give Extract its own chapter: pulling from more than one real source at once.
